title: Competencies Mastered
summary: Identify and categorize core distributed systems competencies, including collective communication modeling, topology selection, and MTBF-based recovery design.

blocks.md:
This lesson follows **Competencies Mastered** in *Conclusion* (Vol II). By the end you should be able to:

- Identify and categorize core distributed systems competencies, including collective communication modeling, topology selection, and MTBF-based recovery design
- Differentiate between infrastructure service health (latency/uptime) and model semantic health (drift/quality) in production operations
- Calculate how cluster Mean Time Between Failures scales with accelerator count under independent component failure models
- Formulate concrete architectural implementations for privacy, fairness, and carbon constraints within distributed training, serving, and orchestration runtimes

The proposed cluster expansion tests competence across the whole stack. Accepting it requires evidence that reduced compute time survives communication and recovery costs, while releasing its model requires a separate serving and governance judgment. Mastery means identifying those dependencies, choosing the measurements that test them, and defending the decision within the stated assumptions. Each band of the stack contributes one checkable part of that defense.

blocks.title: Map of the section
blocks.md: Pay attention to: the three core competency domains: distributed systems, production operations, and governance/ethics; data and concept drift monitoring vs infrastructure performance metrics; cluster MTBF mathematical scaling; governance and sustainability as structural architectural requirements.

blocks.prompt:
Think first: For each of the three governance requirements below, describe one concrete architectural modification that must be built into the production system pipeline rather than handled as a post-hoc audit:
(a) Differential Privacy ((PrivacyBudget, PrivacyAdditiveSlack)) guarantees during training.
(b) Subgroup fairness monitoring during live inference serving.
(c) Carbon-aware scheduling across a multi-region data-center fleet.
blocks.md:
(a) **Differential Privacy**: Define the protected unit and adjacency relation, then incorporate clipping at that unit and calibrated Gaussian noise into the distributed training mechanism, accompanied by a privacy accountant (such as a Rényi DP tracker) that tracks cumulative (PrivacyBudget, PrivacyAdditiveSlack) budget consumption under matching sampling and release assumptions and stops before the authorized budget is exceeded.
(b) **Subgroup Fairness Monitoring**: Instrument the inference serving runtime to collect authorized demographic attributes, or explicitly validated group estimates with uncertainty and coverage limits, alongside model predictions and user outcomes, routing this telemetry into a streaming evaluation pipeline that joins delayed ground-truth outcomes before computing calibration and equal opportunity metrics across demographic cohorts. Selection rates can be tracked before labels arrive; sensitive attributes require access and retention controls.
(c) **Carbon-Aware Scheduling**: Integrate real-time marginal grid carbon intensity APIs (gCO_2eq/kWh) into the cluster orchestrator, using those signals to compare feasible placements and execution windows. Deadline, capacity, data-residency, recovery, transfer, and energy costs must be included before accepting a net-emissions reduction.

questions.q: An ML systems engineer tunes a 2,048-accelerator Ring AllReduce collective around the \$2(DeviceCount-1)CollectivePayloadSize/DeviceCount bandwidth transfer model, chooses how to partition the model across nodes, and configures an automated Young-Daly checkpoint interval based on an observed 4-hour cluster MTBF. Under the chapter's competency framework, which band of the fleet stack does this set of engineering activities belong to?
questions.explanation: The correct answer is C. The Distribution band, because it makes a workload larger than any single machine behave as one coordinated system while designing for routine hardware failure. The chapter organizes competence by the four bands of the fleet stack: Infrastructure, Distribution, Serving, and Governance. Distribution-band competence covers analyzing collective communication, selecting a parallelization strategy, and deriving failure cadence and checkpoint intervals from component MTBF and fleet size. Model architecture research focuses on mathematical layer formulations rather than cluster communication and reliability. Data curation addresses dataset quality rather than network fabrics and checkpointing. Legal auditing concerns statutory compliance rather than network bandwidth and collective communication models.

questions.q: A production recommender system maintains a pristine green status on its operational dashboard, meeting its p99 latency SLO of 45 ms and 99.99% service availability continuously for six months. However, business analytics reveals that user click-through rate (CTR) and conversion revenue have degraded by 18% over the same period. Why does the chapter's production operations competency treat this service as failing despite perfect infrastructure SLOs?
questions.explanation: The correct answer is B. Production operations requires continuous monitoring of data and concept drift alongside performance health; a service that serves stale or degraded predictions at low latency fails its operational mandate. Production operations in ML systems differs fundamentally from traditional web services operations: meeting service-level objectives for uptime, latency, and throughput (performance health) is necessary but insufficient. Because real-world data distributions shift over time (covariate and concept drift), a model can rapidly serve increasingly irrelevant predictions while operating at peak hardware efficiency. Operational mastery demands joint monitoring of systems metrics (latency, QPS, memory) and statistical/semantic metrics (drift detection, feature freshness, downstream conversion). The dashboard and business decline alone do not establish TCP packet loss, concept drift, or any other specific cause. Investigate exposure, feature semantics, delayed outcomes, and product or population changes before attribution. The idea that 45 ms latency causes user distrust is unfounded. Treating CTR as irrelevant ignores the core objective of recommender systems.
questions.hint: Think about: differentiate between infrastructure service health (latency/uptime) and model semantic health (drift/quality) in production operations.
options: Any 18% drop in click-through rate indicates that the underlying network switches are silently dropping TCP packets during feature lookup.

Production operations requires continuous monitoring of data and concept drift alongside performance health; a service that serves stale or degraded predictions at low latency fails its operational mandate.
A 45 ms latency is too fast for human perception, which causes users to distrust the recommendation output and reject the items.
The serving system is operating correctly; click-through rate is an unmeasurable metric that has no relation to ML systems engineering.

questions.q: Assuming identical independent constant component failure rates and that each component failure interrupts the job, in a cluster of DeviceCount accelerators, the cluster mean time between failures decreases inversely with cluster size (SystemMtbf = ComponentMttf/DeviceCount), meaning that doubling cluster size cuts the expected time between training interruptions in half.
questions.explanation: True. Under the stated model of identical independent constant component failure rates, each interrupting the job, the aggregate job failure rate is the sum of the individual failure rates, DeviceCountComponentFailureRate for per-accelerator rate ComponentFailureRate. Because MTBF is the reciprocal of the failure rate, the cluster MTBF scales as SystemMtbf = 1/(DeviceCountComponentFailureRate) = ComponentMttf/DeviceCount. In synchronous training, because any single node failure stalls the global collective, the affected job experiences interruptions at the rate of the components required by this model.
